Keep the gradient from the best run and lower temperature to test whether selectivity improves the lone critical pair (R = 0.82). Its 3.08-minute last peak leaves ample room for increased retention without a time penalty.

Halve the gradient slope while holding the other settings at the best method to test whether the remaining critical pair reaches R ≥ 1.5. The current last peak at 4.49 minutes leaves substantial room to improve separation before incurring a time penalty.

The maximum CRF is achieved; now shorten the fully resolved separation. A 16-minute gradient tests an intermediate slope expected to keep the critical pair near or above R = 1.5 while reducing the last-peak time.
Shorten the gradient by one grid step to locate the full-resolution boundary. If the critical pair falls below R = 1.5, the 16-minute gradient remains the fastest fully resolved method tested.

Test a 5 °C temperature increase to shorten retention, paired with a shallower gradient to compensate for the critical pair’s temperature sensitivity. This may preserve full resolution while bringing the last peak earlier than 5.04 minutes.

The critical pair appears to pass through a selectivity crossover near 30 °C, so test beyond 35 °C rather than assuming warming always worsens separation. Keeping injection 4’s gradient isolates the temperature effect and explores a faster fully resolved method.

Test a steeper gradient at 35 °C, where the critical pair appears to be on the opposite side of its temperature-driven crossover. Steepening may improve that pair’s separation while shortening retention; the other pairs in injection 4 had resolution margins to spare.

Shift the fully resolving 25 °C gradient window upward by 0.05 while preserving its slope to test a faster separation through solvent selectivity. Monitor both the critical pair and early-peak compression; injection 11 remains the fully resolved fallback.

Lower the starting organic fraction to test whether weaker initial solvent improves the critical pair, while steepening the gradient to limit late-peak retention. This explores a different route to a fully resolved separation near or below the current 5.04-minute last-peak time.

Shorten the fastest fully resolved method by one gradient-time step, keeping its solvent window and temperature fixed. The minimum resolution of 1.91 provides some margin to reduce retention while targeting CRF 1.000.

Test the next shorter gradient to bracket the speed limit at this solvent window and temperature. The two closest pairs may fall below R = 1.5; if so, injection 18 remains the fastest fully resolved method tested.

Keep the fastest fully resolved gradient and test 35 °C, beyond the apparent selectivity crossover near 30 °C, to seek shorter retention. The lower starting organic fraction may protect early-pair resolution better than the previous 35–40 °C methods starting at 0.40.

Return to 25 °C and lower the starting organic fraction to improve initial retention and potentially separate the critical middle pair. A steeper gradient offsets the weaker start, testing another route to full resolution near the current fastest last-peak time of 4.14 minutes.

Use a shallower gradient than injection 21 to strengthen the two marginal pairs, with a modest temperature increase to offset added retention. This tests whether the lower starting organic fraction permits full resolution at 30 °C while keeping the last peak near four minutes.

Lengthen injection 22’s gradient by one step to test whether its two marginal middle pairs can both reach R ≥ 1.5. This isolates slope sensitivity at 30 °C while retaining injection 18 as the fastest fully resolved fallback.

Test an intermediate starting fraction at 30 °C with a shallower slope to balance the middle pairs’ opposing selectivity responses. This may restore full resolution with shorter retention than injection 23; injection 18 remains the fastest fully resolved fallback.

Lengthen injection 24’s gradient one step to improve its lone marginal pair while retaining the other pairs’ resolution margins. This final refinement targets another CRF 1.000 method; injection 18 remains the fastest fully resolved method tested.
